source.title: Generalization and Scaling Laws for Mixture-of-Experts Transformers

page_placements.theme: Theoretical compute allocations depend on assumptions and regime

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and figure/table text are flattened or garbled, especially in the appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper extends scaling-law analysis to MoE Transformers, deriving theoretical scaling results and reporting its own validation-loss scaling sweeps in that new architecture setting.
record.gate_note: The paper also discusses scaling results from prior studies, including JMSL and EL; those cited results are not recorded as rows. The retained empirical rows are the paper's own scaling fits and routing ablations, plus its own compute-optimal bound derivation.
record.test_reason: The paper runs its own small MoE decoder-only language-model sweeps on three text corpora. It fits log validation loss against log active parameters and against log tokens. These results bear on V1 in a new architecture setting and, through dataset-dependent exponents, on V7. The compute-optimal result (R7) minimises a theoretical upper bound and is not a measured allocation, so it does not test V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that MoE models show dense-style scaling when measured by active parameters, with routing as a conservative logarithmic overhead. They say observed exponents are only 'of comparable magnitude' to theory, not in tight agreement, and that the regimes studied are far from asymptotic. Routing ablations show a specialization regime at large M/k that the worst-case theory does not capture.
record.recipe_differences: The study combines statistical approximation/generalization theory for MoE Transformers with small-to-medium-scale MoE language-model sweeps; it does not reproduce the original dense-model scaling-law procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that fitted β differs between model-scaling and data-scaling regimes, and that routing effects differ between moderate M/k and sufficiently large M/k.

fits_no_version.finding: Minimising the paper's excess-risk bound under C≃n·Nact gives Nact*∝C^{d/(2β+2d)} and n*∝C^{(2β+d)/(2β+2d)}. Under this bound, data should grow faster than active parameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Worst-case statistical bounds for MoE Transformers imply a compute-optimal split favouring data over active parameters, with error ∝ C^{-β/(β+d)}.

fits_no_version.finding: The smoothness β inferred from model-scaling fits (about 0.5) differs from that inferred from data-scaling fits (1.0–1.5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Intrinsic-dimension scaling theory does not recover a single consistent smoothness parameter across model and data scaling regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed compute, validation loss rises with routing complexity for M/k≤8. Larger expert pools then improve loss again.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed compute, enlarging the expert pool can improve MoE validation loss through specialization even when the worst-case routing-complexity term rises.

record.problems: The authors describe their empirical regime as small-to-medium scale and the asymptotic claims as far from their experimental regime. The scaling-exponent uncertainties are not reported. The empirical loss is called validation loss, but its exact definition is not stated. The compute-optimal allocation is derived from a bound and is not empirically checked in this paper.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified values for the other routing-ablation configurations are stated in the text; those figure-only points are not extracted. Results attributed to prior work in Appendix B are excluded because they are cited or re-analysed prior results rather than this paper's own experiments.

untested.parts: Loss versus compute is not swept. The 'several orders of magnitude' part is untested: Nact spans about 8x and tokens about 16x. Goodness of fit is not reported.
No extrapolation from small to larger runs.
No empirical compute-optimal allocation. Only a bound-minimisation theorem is given, plus re-analysis of JMSL's cited results.
Only text pretraining is studied; there is no other modality, fine-tuning or transfer.
The paper's own runs do not test dependence on parameter counting, schedule or fitting method, disagreement among published laws, or curvature away from a power law.

missing.what: Table 2 empirical exponents (α̂N, α̂D per dataset: WT-103 0.060/0.058; OWT 0.045/0.043 and 0.068/0.062; TinyStories 0.085/0.081). These conflict with the Figure 4/5 labels the rows use.
The authors' own check that empirical exponents approximately satisfy αD ≈ αN/(1+αN) across datasets.

record.verdict_notes: The V3 label was dropped because R7 is a bound-minimisation theorem and its n* exponent was mis-transcribed. The V1 limits_scope label was dropped because small scale and narrow range are untested parts, not qualifications shown by results. The paper's '12 orders of magnitude' claim is contradicted by Table 3. Figure-label exponents and Table 2 exponents disagree, and the flattened figure text may mismatch panels; a researcher should check the PDF figures. The Appendix B JMSL/EL comparisons are re-analyses of cited results and correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: Empirical loss scaling with compute is not swept directly. The empirical measure is reported as validation loss, with its exact loss definition not stated.
No small-run fits are used to predict the loss of much larger runs.
The compute-optimal allocation is derived by minimizing a theoretical excess-risk bound under C ≃ n·Nact; the paper does not empirically verify the resulting allocation on its own training runs.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The experiments concern text language models; other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
The paper does not empirically establish disagreement among published laws or demonstrate curves bending away from a single power law. Its comparisons to prior studies rely on their reported results.

rows.subject: MoE Transformer theoretical class
rows.size_stated: Active parameter budget Nact; size not otherwise stated.
rows.operation_detail: Minimize the theoretical excess-error bound subject to the compute proxy C ≃ n·Nact.
rows.measure: Compute-optimal growth exponents for active parameters and sample size
rows.note: This is a theorem about minimizing the paper's bound, not an empirical measurement of a trained model's loss-minimizing allocation.
rows.check: This row is a theorem minimising an upper bound, not a measured loss-minimising allocation. Its value is also mis-transcribed: Eq. 18 gives n*(C) ≃ C^{(2β+d)/(2β+2d)}, not C^{d/(2β+2d)}. So under the bound, data grows faster than active parameters, not equally.

source_check.correct: Nact*(C) ≃ C^{d/(2β+2d)}; n*(C) ≃ C^{(2β+d)/(2β+2d)}; excess-error bound ≃ C^{-β/(β+d)}. These minimize the theoretical bound under C ≃ nNact.

rows.subject: MoE decoder-only Transformer language models
rows.operation_detail: Compare effective smoothness estimates inferred from model-scaling and data-scaling fits.
rows.measure: Agreement of fitted exponents / inferred β across scaling regimes
rows.value: The inferred β values do not coincide exactly; model fits are most consistent with β = 0.5 across datasets, while data fits are most consistent with β = 1.5 for OpenWebText and β = 1.0 for TinyStories and WikiText-103.
rows.note: The authors attribute the mismatch to the regimes probing different error components and to optimization noise, finite-sample effects, and routing overhead.
rows.check: This row compares the paper's own theory parameter β inferred from two regimes. It checks internal consistency of the theory, not dependence of published scaling laws on setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: MoE decoder-only Transformer language models

rows.measure: Validation loss as routing complexity k log(eM/k) varies
rows.value: Validation loss increases approximately monotonically with the routing term.
rows.note: This is a routing-complexity result, not a direct test of any listed scaling-law version.
rows.check: This is a routing-complexity result and does not bear on the listed versions.
